findings.title: Test assertion insufficient for intended scenario
findings.rationale: The test claims to verify 'scans using the registry default when no workspace override is saved', but the only assertion is `expect(res.statusCode).toBe(202)`. A 202 status could be returned even if the server silently uses a fallback model or errors internally. The test would not catch a regression where the default model is ignored or the endpoint returns a success code with wrong behavior. To cover the intent, the test should assert on the response body (e.g., the model used) or on database records after the scan.

findings.title: Test assertion does not verify the core behaviour (default model selection)
findings.rationale: The test's only assertion is that the endpoint responds with 202. It does not verify that the extraction actually used the registry's default model (the stated goal). A production code change that ignores model resolution entirely—e.g., always returning 202 with a dummy extraction—would still pass this test. To guard the intended behaviour, the test should assert something about the resolved model, such as checking the extraction's stored model name in the database or inspecting a response payload if the endpoint were synchronous.

findings.title: Test does not verify the model resolution it claims to test
findings.rationale: The test claims to verify that the scan uses the registry default model when no workspace override is saved, but the only assertion is `expect(res.statusCode).toBe(202)`. It does not check which model was used for extraction. A production bug that selects the wrong model (e.g., always hardcoding a different model) but still returns 202 would not be caught. The test cannot fail for the intended behavior, only for crashes.

findings.title: Missing test for the workspace‑override branch and error path
findings.rationale: The test only covers the case where no workspace override exists. It does not cover the symmetric case (workspace has an override), nor does it verify error behavior when the registry has no default model. The PR description frames the test as covering a specific path, but the single happy‑path test leaves the other branches of the same logic uncovered. (Note: this is a suggestion because only the added test file is in scope, but testing the other side would improve coverage.)

findings.title: Missing verification of model selection in workspace override test
findings.rationale: The test's only assertion checks that the HTTP status code is 202, but it does not verify that the extraction was actually performed using the registry's default model. findings.title: GROUP BY not exercised — single PR hides regression
findings.rationale: The test only inserts rows for a single pull request.  A production regression that accidentally drops the `GROUP BY pr_id` clause would still return the correct sum for a single PR, so the test would pass.  To guard against that regression the test should insert runs for at least two different PRs and assert that the query returns separate (or aggregated) rows per PR.

findings.title: Silent skip when Docker is unavailable
findings.rationale: When Docker is unavailable the test returns early via `if (!pg) return;`.  That early return contains no assertion, so the test passes regardless of the production code's correctness.  A developer who runs tests without Docker would see green and incorrectly believe the cost-total logic is verified.  While this pattern is common, the test-smells rule warns about a test that 'cannot fail' for a significant class of failures.

findings.title: Silent skip when Docker unavailable
findings.rationale: The test silently passes when Docker is unavailable without executing any assertions. A failure in the test setup (e.g., a regression in the fixture) would not be caught in environments without Docker, giving false confidence.

findings.title: Grouping behavior not validated
findings.rationale: The test inserts runs only for a single PR and filters directly by that PR's ID. It does not verify that `SUM(cost_usd) GROUP BY pr_id` correctly separates totals across different PRs. A production bug that drops the GROUP BY clause or alters filtering would still pass this test because only one PR's data exists. To catch grouping bugs, the test should insert runs for at least two different PRs and assert that each PR's total is correct.

matched_title: Test assertion contradicts expected column behaviour

findings.title: Test assertion contradicts expected column behaviour
findings.rationale: The test inserts an agent_run without specifying retryCount, so the column defaults to null. The assertion `expect(row.retryCount).not.toBeNull()` expects a non-null value, but the correct value is null. This means the test will fail on a correct implementation (blocking CI) and does not actually prove the column round-trips properly—it only proves a mistaken expectation. To verify the column exists and can be read, either assert `expect(row.retryCount).toBeNull()` (matching the no-retry scenario) or assert that the value is `null | number` (e.g., `expect(typeof row.retryCount).toBe('number')` after inserting a run with a specific retry_count).

matched_title: Test's only assertion is insufficient to verify column round-trip

findings.title: Test's only assertion is insufficient to verify column round-trip
findings.rationale: The row is inserted without setting `retryCount` (a nullable column with no default), so the database returns `null`. `expect(row.retryCount).not.toBeNull()` will fail, proving nothing about the column's ability to store and retrieve a value. Additionally, even if a value were inserted, `not.toBeNull()` alone does not verify that the correct value was stored—a 'round-trip' test demands an equality assertion on a known value.

findings.title: Test assertion contradicts schema – column is nullable but test expects not null with no value provided
findings.rationale: The test inserts a row without providing retryCount, then asserts row.retryCount is not null (line 19). Because the schema defines retryCount as nullable with no default, the column will always be null in the database. This assertion will always fail, so the test is broken and does not validate round-trip of a retry count value as claimed by the PR description. If the production code later adds a default or makes the column not null, this test could pass without actually testing that a stored value round-trips correctly.

matched_title: Test uses an assertion that cannot guard the column's presence

findings.title: Test uses an assertion that cannot guard the column's presence
findings.rationale: The test asserts `expect(row.retryCount).not.toBeNull()` on a nullable column that was left unset during insert. With the current schema this assertion fails (the column is null), so the test is broken. Worse, if the column were removed entirely, Drizzle would return `undefined` for the missing property, and `expect(undefined).not.toBeNull()` passes — meaning the test would greenlight a change that drops the column. The test does not actually verify a round‑trip value; it should insert a known `retryCount` and assert equality.

matched_title: Repository methods vulnerable to SQL injection and completely untested

findings.title: Repository methods vulnerable to SQL injection and completely untested
findings.rationale: Repository methods `findByToken`, `list`, `getDigestBody`, and `insert` interpolate user-controlled values directly into SQL via `sql.raw(...)` instead of using parameterized queries. No test exercises any of these methods, so the SQL injection vulnerabilities, which allow an attacker to read or modify the database, would never be caught. A test that passes a malicious token (e.g., `' OR '1'='1`) would expose the injection by causing a different result or an SQL error.

findings.title: Command injection in exportDigest and snapshotExports, no tests exist
findings.rationale: `exportDigest` and `snapshotExports` pass user-controlled values (`digestId` and `label`) directly to `execSync` without sanitization. No test exercises these functions, so command injection vulnerabilities — which let an attacker execute arbitrary shell commands on the server — would go undetected. A test passing a `digestId` like `; rm -rf /` would prove the issue.

findings.title: Unsafe code evaluation in renderTemplate with zero tests
findings.rationale: `renderTemplate` uses `new Function(...keys, \`return (${expr});\`)` to evaluate arbitrary expressions from the digest body. Without any test, the code-injection risk — where an attacker could craft a digest with a malicious `{{ ... }}` expression to execute arbitrary code — is completely unguarded. A test that passes a template containing `{{ process.env.SECRET }}` would expose the leak.

findings.title: Shared digest resolution entirely untested — access control gaps
findings.rationale: `getSharedDigest` throws `NotFoundError` when the token is not found, which produces a 404. No test confirms that this error path works correctly or that the error message does not leak internals. More critically, the entire function — which controls access to shared digest content — has no test at all. A regression that breaks token resolution or the template rendering would silently pass.

findings.title: No test for missing-digest path in exportDigest
findings.rationale: `exportDigest` throws `NotFoundError` when the digest does not exist, but no test triggers this path. SQL injection in `getDigestBody` (see finding 1) compounds the lack of coverage. A change that accidentally makes the error always fire or never fire would pass undetected.

findings.title: Snapshot API failure path totally untested
findings.rationale: `snapshotExports` throws `AppError` when the maintenance API returns a non-ok status. No test covers this error recovery branch. Without a test, a regression that makes the snapshot silently fail (no error thrown) would not be caught, potentially leaving the system without backups.

findings.title: Client component SharedDigestView completely untested — no test covers any UI state
findings.rationale: `SharedDigestView` has three branches (error, loading, success) but no test exercises any of them. The component fetches from an API and uses `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` — any changes to the API response shape or the error handling logic would go undetected because no test exists. Missing tests also mean the XSS risk of `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` (if `digest.html` ever contains untrusted data) is unguarded.

matched_title: New exported function with no test: generateShareToken

findings.title: New exported function with no test: generateShareToken
findings.rationale: `generateShareToken` is an exported function with zero test coverage. A broken token generation (e.g., collision, non‑unique tokens, or wrong length) would ship undetected. Token minting is the security root of the entire share‑link feature.

findings.title: New exported function with no test: renderTemplate
findings.rationale: `renderTemplate` uses `new Function(...)` to evaluate arbitrary expressions against a scope. Without a unit test that exercises this function with various expression strings, a malformed expression or one that accesses the global scope would not be caught. This is especially dangerous because the scope comes from query parameters (`req.query`) which the end user controls.

findings.title: No test covers SQL injection in ShareRepository.findByToken
findings.rationale: `findByToken` interpolates the `token` parameter directly into a SQL string without parameterisation. This is a critical security vulnerability that would allow SQL injection. No test exists that exercises this method, so the injection path would ship undetected. Because the token is user‑supplied (via the URL route parameter) and the only access control for the share, this is a critical test gap.

findings.title: No test covers SQL injection in ShareRepository.list
findings.rationale: `ShareRepository.list` interpolates a `sort` parameter directly into `ORDER BY ${sort}`. The `sort` value comes from an HTTP query parameter with no validation or escaping. This is a SQL injection vector. No test covers this method.

findings.title: No test covers SQL injection in ShareRepository.getDigestBody
findings.rationale: `getDigestBody` interpolates the `digestId` parameter directly into a SQL string. Same injection risk as the other repository methods. No test covers this method.

findings.title: No test covers SQL injection in ShareRepository.insert
findings.rationale: `insert` interpolates `digestId`, `token`, and `passwordHash` directly into a SQL string. Attackers who control any of these values (e.g. through `POST /digests/:id/share` body) can inject SQL. No test covers this method.

findings.title: No test covers command injection in ShareService.exportDigest
findings.rationale: `exportDigest` uses `execSync` with the `digestId` parameter interpolated directly into a shell command. If an attacker controls `digestId` (e.g. via `POST /digests/:id/export`), they can execute arbitrary shell commands. No test covers this method, so this command injection vulnerability would go undetected.

findings.title: No test covers ShareService.snapshotExports
findings.rationale: `snapshotExports` shells out with the `label` parameter without validation. If the label is user‑controlled, this is a command injection vector. Additionally, it calls an internal maintenance API with a hardcoded token that is stored in plaintext in the source code. No test covers this method, so a failure in the snapshot process would not be caught.

findings.title: New client component with no test
findings.rationale: `SharedDigestView` is a new exported React component with all its states (loading, error, success) untested. The component fetches from the API and uses `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` with server‑returned HTML; without a test that confirms the API response shape and that the HTML is sanitised, XSS vulnerabilities could ship.

findings.title: Command Injection in `exportDigest` und `snapshotExports`
findings.rationale: Führen Sie einen Command-Injection-Angriff durch, indem Sie die Parameter `digestId` oder `format` manipulieren: Der Aufruf `execSync("mkdir -p ${EXPORT_DIR} && tar -czf ${target} -C ${EXPORT_DIR} ${digestId}")` interpoliert ungeprüfte Benutzereingaben direkt in die Shell, was das Ausführen beliebiger Kommandos ermöglicht.

findings.title: SQL Injection in `ShareRepository.findByToken` und `ShareRepository.list`
findings.rationale: Die Methode `findByToken` und andere Methoden in `ShareRepository` verwenden `sql.raw()` mit direkter String-Interpolation von Benutzereingaben (`'${token}'`), was eine klassische SQL-Injection-Lücke darstellt. Ein Angreifer kann die Datenbank manipulieren oder auslesen.

findings.title: Arbitrary Code Execution durch `new Function` in `renderTemplate`
findings.rationale: Die Funktion `renderTemplate` verwendet `new Function(...keys, ...)` mit Ausdrücken aus der Benutzereingabe (wenn die Scope-Daten oder der Body bösartig sind). Dies ermöglicht die Ausführung beliebigen JavaScript-Codes im Serverkontext (Arbitrary Code Execution).

findings.title: Hartcodierte Geheimnisse in `constants.ts`
findings.rationale: Geheimer HMAC-Schlüssel (`SHARE_SIGNING_SECRET`) und Wartungs-API-Token (`MAINTENANCE_API_TOKEN`) sind hartcodiert und im Klartext im Quellcode gespeichert. Dies verstößt gegen das Prinzip der Geheimnisverwaltung (Secret Management) und ermöglicht jedem mit Zugriff auf den Code, Token zu fälschen oder auf die Wartungs-API zuzugreifen.

findings.title: Verwendung des unsicheren MD5-Hash in `hashSharePassword`
findings.rationale: Die Funktion `hashSharePassword` verwendet MD5, das als kryptografisch unsicher gilt (Kollisionsanfälligkeit, Rainbow-Table-Angriffe). Ein Angreifer, der die Datenbank kompromittiert, kann Passwörter leicht reverse-engineeren.

findings.title: Path Traversal in `/share/:token/attachment` Route
findings.rationale: Der Route `/share/:token/attachment` (`GET`) übergibt den Query-Parameter `name` direkt an `service.readExport`, der ihn in `readFileSync(join(EXPORT_DIR, name))` verwendet. Ein Path-Traversal-Angriff über `../` ist möglich (z.B. `/share/token/attachment?name=../../etc/passwd`), der es erlaubt, beliebige Dateien des Servers auszulesen.

findings.title: Command Injection und SSRF in `snapshotExports`
findings.rationale: In `snapshotExports` wird der Parameter `label` ungeprüft in der Shell verwendet (`tar -czf /var/app/snapshots/${label}.tgz ...`). Ein Angreifer, der den Admin-Endpunkt erreicht, kann beliebige Kommandos ausführen. Zudem wird die interne Maintenance-API mit einem hartcodierten Bearer-Token aufgerufen – ein SSRF-Angriff wäre denkbar.

findings.title: Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) in `unfurl`
findings.rationale: Die Funktion `unfurl` ruft `fetch(url)` mit einer beliebigen, vom Benutzer kommenden URL auf (aus `POST /share/preview`). Dies ermöglicht Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF). Ein Angreifer kann interne Dienste (z.B. `http://localhost:5432`, `http://10.0.0.5:8080/admin`) scannen oder manipulieren.

findings.title: XSS-Risiko durch `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` in `SharedDigestView`
findings.rationale: Die Komponente `SharedDigestView` rendert serverseitig erzeugtes HTML mittels `dangerouslySetInnerHTML`. Wenn die API kompromittiert ist oder ein XSS-Angriff auf die Digest-Inhalte erfolgt, wird der Schadcode im Browser ausgeführt. Zudem wird der HTML-Inhalt nicht validiert – selbst wenn er vom Server kommt, besteht bei fehlerhafter Markdown-Konvertierung XSS-Risiko.

findings.title: Schwache Token-Generierung mit `Math.random()`
findings.rationale: Die Funktion `generateShareToken` verwendet `Math.random()`, das nicht kryptografisch sicher ist (kann vorhersagbar sein). Ein Angreifer könnte die Token-Sequenz vorhersagen und sich unberechtigten Zugriff verschaffen.

findings.title: Open Redirect in `/share/login/callback`
findings.rationale: Die Route `/share/login/callback` (`GET`) leitet den Benutzer an den Wert des `next`-Query-Paramethers weiter, ohne ihn zu validieren. Dies ermöglicht einen Open Redirect-Angriff, bei dem ein Angreifer einen Benutzer auf eine bösartige Seite umleiten kann (Phishing).

findings.title: Unverschlüsselte interne Kommunikation
findings.rationale: Die Variable `MAINTENANCE_API_URL` (`http://10.0.0.5:8080/admin`) zeigt auf eine interne IP-Adresse über unverschlüsseltes HTTP. Ein Angreifer im selben Netzwerk kann die Kommunikation abhören oder manipulieren (Man-in-the-Middle).

matched_title: SQL injection in all repository methods is untested

findings.title: SQL injection in all repository methods is untested
findings.rationale: All four repository methods (`findByToken`, `list`, `getDigestBody`, `insert`) concatenate user‑controlled strings directly into SQL via `sql.raw`. This is a textbook SQL injection vulnerability that no test exercises. A test with a malicious token (`' OR 1=1 --`) would immediately fail, proving the code is vulnerable, but the total absence of tests means this defect would ship unchecked.

findings.title: Command injection in exportDigest and snapshotExports is untested
findings.rationale: `exportDigest` and `snapshotExports` concatenate user‑supplied `digestId` and `label` into shell commands via `execSync`. Without tests that try values like `; rm -rf /` or `$(id)`, the command injection vulnerability is invisible to CI. The missing test branch is critical because it guards a privilege escalation path.

findings.title: Unsafe code evaluation in renderTemplate has no security test
findings.rationale: `renderTemplate` uses `new Function(...)` to evaluate template expressions like `{{ repo.stars * 2 }}`. An attacker who controls the digest body or the template scope can inject arbitrary JavaScript. No test validates that sandboxing prevents access to `globalThis`, `process`, or `require`. This untested branch is critical because it skips the security check that would typically prevent JS execution in a template engine.

findings.title: No test verifies authentication is required for creating a share
findings.rationale: The `POST /digests/:id/share` route calls `getContext(app.container, req)` to authenticate the user, and the route returns 201 on success. There is no test that sends a request without valid credentials and asserts a 401/403. An untested auth gate is critical because a configuration mistake or a future refactor could remove the auth call without a failing test.

findings.title: Failed maintenance API response branch in snapshotExports is untested
findings.rationale: In `snapshotExports`, if the maintenance API responds with a non‑ok status, the code throws an `AppError`. No test exercises this branch. An untested error path in a scheduled maintenance operation means a silent failure (the snapshot archive is created but never registered) would go undetected during CI.

findings.title: Error state in SharedDigestView is never tested
findings.rationale: The `catch` block in `SharedDigestView` sets `error` state when the fetch fails or the API returns a non‑ok status. No unit test verifies that a network error or an unexpected API response renders the correct error message. Because the test infrastructure mocks `fetch`, a test could easily simulate an error response and assert the UI shows "Link expired", yet no such test exists. The missing branch is a warning—the error is displayed to the user, not a security issue, but it is changed logic that would not fail CI.

findings.title: Missing digest/share link not found paths are untested
findings.rationale: `exportDigest` and `getSharedDigest` both have an `if (!row) throw NotFoundError` branch. No test provides a non‑existent digest or share token and asserts that a 404 is returned. An untested missing‑resource branch is a warning: the error behaviour is business logic that would not be caught by CI.
